pages.text: Robin Hood is the great outlaw hero of English legend: a man who lives in the forest, outside the law, and uses his extraordinary skill with a bow to protect the poor from the powerful. He is not a king or a knight. He is, by the standards of those who rule, a criminal. That is precisely the point.

image.note: Illustration: Robin Hood in Lincoln green beneath an ancient oak in Sherwood Forest, bow in hand

pages.text: No one knows whether Robin Hood was a real person. Records from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries mention an outlaw called Robert Hood or Robert of Loxley, but the stories attached to those names grew far beyond any historical individual. By the fifteenth century, the legends were fully formed: Sherwood Forest, the Merry Men, the Sheriff of Nottingham, Maid Marian, and the signature phrase that has echoed across eight centuries: rob from the rich and give to the poor.

The Robin Hood stories have survived because they speak to something universal: the feeling that the powerful protect each other, that the law serves wealth rather than justice, and that someone, somewhere, ought to do something about it. Different ages have told the Robin Hood story differently, but the core has remained constant: a man who chooses the right side over the legal side.

Robert of Loxley was a young nobleman whose land was seized while he was away at the Crusades. Returning to find himself without property and without rights, he was declared an outlaw, which in medieval law meant that anyone could kill him without legal consequence. He went to Sherwood Forest.

image.note: Illustration: Robert of Loxley arriving at a burned-out manor, a legal notice nailed to the gate

pages.text: In the forest he met Little John, a giant of a man who defeated him in a staff fight on a log bridge and then laughed so warmly at the result that they became friends. He met Friar Tuck, a fat and jovial friar with a surprisingly violent temper and a deep knowledge of scripture and wine in approximately equal measure. He met Will Scarlet and Much the Miller's Son and eventually a band of outlaws who had all, in different ways, been failed by the law.

They lived well in the forest. They hunted the king's deer, which was illegal. They robbed wealthy travellers on the road north from London, which was also illegal. They gave what they took to the farmers and villagers who had been taxed into destitution by the Sheriff of Nottingham. This was technically illegal too. They did not appear to mind.

The tale of how Robin met Little John is told at every telling, for it shows the kind of man Robin was. Crossing a stream on a narrow log bridge, Robin met a giant of a stranger coming the other way, and neither would step aside for the other. They fought with quarterstaffs there on the log, blow for blow, until the stranger knocked Robin clean into the water. Instead of anger, Robin roared with laughter, and offered the stranger a place among his men.

The giant's name was John Little, and Robin's men, with the humour of outlaws, at once renamed him Little John, and Little John he stayed. He became Robin's most loyal companion and his equal in a fight. The meeting tells you everything: Robin lost, and laughed, and made a friend of the man who beat him. An outlaw who could do that was a leader men would follow into any danger, and they did.

The Sheriff of Nottingham despised Robin Hood not primarily because Robin was an outlaw, but because Robin made him look foolish. Every attempt to capture him ended in humiliation. The Sheriff was not a stupid man, which made this worse.

image.note: Illustration: the Sheriff at his desk, a letter from the King demanding he deal with Robin Hood

pages.text: The Sheriff organised an archery competition in Nottingham, offering a golden arrow to the winner, knowing that Robin Hood, the finest archer in England, would be unable to resist. Robin disguised himself and won the golden arrow. The Sheriff discovered only afterwards that the strange archer who had bested everyone was Robin Hood. The golden arrow arrived at Nottingham Castle by arrow shortly after Robin left, with a note attached.

Every disguise Robin wore, every encounter he engineered with the Sheriff, followed the same pattern: the powerful man, with all his legal authority and armed men, outwitted by the man with nothing but his wits, his skill, and his knowledge of the forest. It is a deeply satisfying pattern. Stories tend to produce the endings their audiences need most.

Maid Marian appears in later versions of the legend. In some accounts she is a noblewoman who loves Robin and visits the forest. In others she is a person of independent strength and intelligence who makes her own decisions. The versions that have proved most durable are the ones in which Marian is not simply waiting to be rescued but is actively choosing her path.

image.note: Illustration: Marian in the forest, dressed for travel, clearly on her own terms

pages.text: She chooses the outlaw over the comfortable life at court. This choice matters as much as Robin's own. A story in which the significant woman has no agency is a lesser story than one in which she does. The best Robin Hood stories understand this.

Robin Hood's world was a real one, and knowing it makes the tales richer. In medieval England the great forests belonged to the king, and the deer in them were his alone. For a starving peasant to take one was a crime punished with terrible cruelty. The law protected the powerful and pressed hardest on the poor, and taxes fell heaviest on those who could least pay. Into that unfairness rides Robin, taking from the rich and giving to the poor, doing by outlawry what the law would not do: justice.

That is why Robin Hood has never died. Every age has felt that the powerful protect one another and that the ordinary person is squeezed, and every age has longed for someone bold enough to even the account. Robin is that longing given a green coat and a bow. He is not real, and it does not matter that he is not real. He stands for something people have always needed to believe: that unfairness can be fought, and that a clever, brave outsider can win.

In the oldest versions of the legend, Robin Hood grows old and ill. He goes to Kirklees Priory, where his cousin the prioress is known for her skill in medicine, and asks to be bled, a common medieval treatment. The prioress, who has reasons of her own, bleeds him too much and leaves him to die.

image.note: Illustration: Robin Hood at a window of a priory, weak but still holding his bow

pages.text: Robin calls for Little John. Little John comes. Robin asks for his bow. He shoots one last arrow through the window and says: bury me where the arrow falls. Little John carries him to the window and sets him down. Robin shoots. The arrow falls in the forest, under a green canopy of leaves.

It is a good death for a man who lived among trees. And because he is a legend, he does not stay dead. King Richard will need him again. The poor will need him again. He will be back, as he always is, whenever the law forgets what it is for.
